canonical_topic: Transmission losses and the voltage trade-off
definition: Power lost as heat during transmission is proportional to the current flowing on the line; raising voltage lowers current for the same power delivered, which reduces losses, but higher voltage lines are more dangerous and can't be sited everywhere.
core_idea: Line losses create an engineering-economic trade-off: utilities want higher voltage to cut losses, but safety and siting constraints limit how high voltage can go in a given location.
key_points: Transmission losses are proportional to current, not directly to power.
Increasing voltage reduces current (for a given power level), which reduces losses.
Higher-voltage lines are more dangerous, restricting where they can be used.
relationships: Directly connects to the choice between high-voltage transmission and low-voltage distribution.
trading_implications: Transmission losses and voltage/siting constraints help explain persistent regional price differences that create wheeling opportunities.
